title: Bless the Lord, O my soul (Psalm 102 [103])
hookLine: he knows we are dust, and his mercy is from eternity

lines: COME ON. YOU CAN DO THIS.
cards: Have you ever talked to yourself out loud? Come on. You can do this.
Don't forget your keys. Most people do it, usually under their breath, in the car or the kitchen. It's how you get your own attention.

The psalms do it too. Several times, the one praying stops talking to God and turns to their own soul, like giving yourself a nudge. One psalm's opening is nothing but that: a pep talk to the self, about gratitude.

teach.b: Psalm 102 in the Douay, 103 in most Bibles: "Bless the Lord, O my soul: and let all that is within me bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and never forget all he hath done for thee."
The Hebrew word for soul here, nephesh, doesn't mean a ghostly inner part. It means your whole living self, even your throat, your breath. So: all of me, wake up and remember.

Why the reminder? Because we forget good things fast. The psalm makes a list: he forgives, he heals, he redeems your life from destruction, he crowns you with mercy, he renews your youth like an eagle's.
Then come the tenderest lines about God in the whole psalter.

teach.h: AS FAR AS THE EAST FROM THE WEST.
teach.b: "As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our iniquities from us." East and west never meet; walk forever and you'll never reach where your sins went.

teach.h: HE REMEMBERETH THAT WE ARE DUST.
teach.b: "As a father hath compassion on his children, so hath the Lord compassion on them that fear him: for he knoweth our frame. He remembereth that we are dust." Not to shame us, but to go easy on us.

Then our shortness again, like the psalm of Moses: "Man's days are as grass." A wind passes over the flower and it's gone. "But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity upon them that fear him."

teach.h: THE FLOWER IS SHORT, MERCY ISN'T.
teach.b: The flower is short. The mercy isn't. At the end it turns outward, angels, heavenly hosts, all his works, bless the Lord, then comes home: bless the Lord, O my soul.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 102 [103] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it often at Mass as a responsorial psalm of mercy, with the refrain drawn from its line that the Lord is kind and merciful.

o: the mind, the part of you that thinks
your whole living self, breath and all
a ghost-like spirit that leaves the body

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: the soul: your whole living self
how far he removes our sins

s: in this psalm, soul means a ghostly inner part
the Hebrew nephesh means your whole living self, even your breath.
the psalm says God remembers we are dust, to go easy on us
as a father has compassion on his children.
the psalm says mercy is as short as a flower
our days are as grass, but the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity.

games.q: you're tired, and all you can see is what's gone wrong. what does the psalmist do in that moment?
o: talk to his own soul: bless the Lord, and never forget all he hath done.
games.why: bless the Lord, O my soul, and never forget all he hath done for thee. the psalm gives itself a nudge toward gratitude.

practice: Talk to yourself a little, the way the psalm does, come on, soul, remember, and find three good things from the past few days: not big ones, a meal, a text from a friend, a moment of sun, a thing that didn't go wrong.
Name each one slowly and stay with it for a few breaths. If you pray, thank God for each, bless the Lord, O my soul; if you don't, let each one land fully before moving on.

wordCard.voice: Nephesh. The Hebrew word for soul: not a ghostly inner part, but your whole living self, breath and all. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: bless, O my soul, the psalm's opening words.

carryVoice: Your line: forget not his benefits. All that is within me, awake. See you tomorrow.
